title: TrackTok: Semantically Persistent Tokens for Latent Video Generation
claim: A video is compressed into a compact set of persistent object-aligned tokens by clustering semantic features into queries, then decoded back.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right, encoder in rounded box, snowflake and flame icons
description: A single left-to-right pipeline diagram. An input video, a stack of frames showing a basketball player against a red wall, passes through a frozen (snowflake) V-JEPA 2.1 feature extractor. This produces a grid of colorful semantic feature maps, shown as a patch grid and as a stack of feature tokens F. A k-Means step goes upward to a cluster map C, where dotted outlines mark the player and other regions. Arrows labeled with centroid c_i point from the clusters to colored query tokens Q, which are numbered 0 and 1 per cluster. Features and queries both enter a tall vertical Vision Transformer bar with a flame (trainable) icon. That bar outputs a column of blue latent tokens Z. These go to a Decoder D bar, which outputs patches P and RGB patches, then a reconstructed video. The encoder sits inside a light-blue rounded box, and the pink and blue palette draws the eye first.
caption: Method Overview. \ours encodes an input video $V$ into a 1D set of object-aligned, semantically persistent, latent tokens $\mathcal{Z}$. Its encoder $\mathcal{E}$ is composed of semantic feature extraction with V-JEPA 2.1 [ref], the construction of input-dependent queries $\mathcal{Q}$ using centroids of $k$-Means clusters $\mathcal{C}$, and a ViT performing attention based on semantic similarity instead of spatial position. The decoder $\mathcal{D}$ reconstructs the three-dimensional RGB video from the 1D latent set $\mathcal{Z}$.
abstract: We introduce TrackTok, an efficient video tokenization framework that produces object-aligned tokens, i.e., tokens that consistently encode the same semantic object across time, even as it moves, deforms, or undergoes partial occlusion. Conventional patch-based or existing holistic tokenizers produce token identities often tied to fixed image locations. In contrast, our approach learns temporally persistent object-aligned representations that bind visual features across frames into stable semantic units. This enables substantially more compact, continuous latent video representations, reducing the number of tokens required for downstream generative modeling with state-of-the-art flow models, while preserving the semantic structure needed for high-quality synthesis. Our tokenizer offers a favorable quality-efficiency trade-off. TrackTok achieves comparable class-conditional generative FVD on UCF-101 dataset at 8 times fewer latent tokens and better latency, and outperforms existing 1D tokenization baselines on frame prediction task on Kinetics-600 across low token budgets. These results suggest that object-aligned and temporally persistent tokenization is a promising direction for scalable video generation, where reducing latent token counts is critical for efficient modeling. Our code for this work is available at github.com/phamleyennhi/tracktok.
